references.text: Pharaoh orders the work to be made harder for the Israelites, leading the overseers to come and complain
The context that led to the Israelite overseers being beaten and then going to Pharaoh to complain
The Israelites groaned and cried out under slavery, an earlier example of the people crying out in distress
God hears the Israelites' cry because of their slave drivers, which connects to the outcry of the overseers
Moses appoints seventy elders as overseers over Israel, showing the role of Israelite leaders and overseers
Instructions to appoint judges and overseers, demonstrating the continued role of שֹׁטְרִים (overseers) in Israel
Both verses center on the theological requirement that Israel's only legitimate service is toward God, creating a clear contrast between human oppression and divine freedom.
Both verses illustrate how resistance to God's plan creates unrest and fear among both the oppressed Israelites and within Pharaoh's own court.
The verses form a continuous dialogue where the overseers' complaint to Pharaoh (v.15) is immediately followed by their blame of Moses for worsening the situation (v.21).

Both verses capture moments when figures around Pharaoh reflect on the consequences of letting Israel go, but with opposite emotions: complaining about oppression versus panicking over the loss of labor.
The verses create a theological contrast between complaining about human oppression (Exodus) and confessing one's own sin as the cause of suffering (Judges).
